meta: Digital X-ray PACS for CR and DR: go filmless, archive every exposure on your own node, let OPD doctors open the image in a browser and send it to the patient.
h1: Digital X-ray PACS: go filmless and let the OPD doctor see the image in a browser.
sub: A digital X-ray unit produces one or a few large images per exam. AuraPACS receives them from the CR reader or DR panel, stores them on a node in your clinic, opens them in any browser for the OPD doctor and sends the image and report to the patient on WhatsApp instead of a film envelope.

persona: Owner of a clinic, polyclinic or small hospital with a CR or DR X-ray unit still printing film

sections.h2: What a digital X-ray PACS does
paras: A digital X-ray PACS takes the image from your CR reader or DR panel over the network, stores it against the patient, and shows it on any screen that needs it. AuraPACS does this on an on-premise node, so the orthopaedic OPD three rooms away opens the chest or knee X-ray in a browser seconds after exposure, and the patient receives it on WhatsApp instead of carrying a film.

X-ray is the simplest modality for a PACS and the one where going filmless pays back fastest. Each exam is one or a few large images rather than a stack of slices, so the archive grows slowly and the viewing is quick even on a modest laptop.

sections.h2: The DR panel is digital. The rest of the workflow is not.
sections.lead: Many clinics bought a digital X-ray unit and then kept printing film because there was nowhere to put the image.

items.p: Each X-ray is printed, sleeved and handed over, at a cost per sheet, even for a routine follow-up.

items.h: The image lives on the acquisition PC
items.p: The only digital copy sits on the CR or DR console, which nobody backs up and which will one day be replaced.

items.h: OPD doctors walk to the X-ray room
items.p: The physician either waits for the film or goes to the console to look at the screen.
The follow-up visit begins with a search for last month's envelope, then a repeat exposure.
Where a radiologist reports, the report is a separate paper unconnected to the digital image.

sections.h2: From exposure to the doctor's screen.

steps.p: Front desk registers the patient and the view; the entry reaches the X-ray worklist.
The technician selects the patient on the CR or DR console; no retyping.
The image is sent as DICOM to the node and filed automatically.
The doctor opens the patient's study in a browser in the consulting room.
A radiologist reports on an X-ray template, finalised to a PDF on the study.
A secure WhatsApp link replaces the film envelope.

items.q: Does it work with a CR reader as well as a DR panel?
items.a: Yes. Both send DICOM images over the network, and both are pointed at the AuraPACS node the same way. Which unit you have is confirmed on a call before setup.

items.q: Can we stop printing film completely?
items.a: Most clinics do. The image is on the node for every OPD doctor, the patient gets a WhatsApp link, and a film is printed only when someone specifically asks. Whether you keep a printer for those cases is your call.

items.q: Do OPD doctors need any software?
items.a: No. The viewer runs in a standard browser on any PC on the clinic network. Each doctor has a login with role-based access, and every view is audited. See DICOM viewer.

items.q: What does the patient receive on WhatsApp?
items.a: A secure link that opens the X-ray image and, where one has been written, the report PDF, with no app or login needed at their end. See WhatsApp report sharing.

items.q: How much storage do X-rays need?
items.a: Less than CT or MR, because each exam is one or a few images rather than a stack. The archive sits on your own node and is sized to your daily volume on a call.
No. It stores, displays and shares the images. The interpretation is by your doctor or radiologist.
